extracted.intended_audience: aspiring fiction writers seeking craft and publication advice
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, craft-focused guidance for fiction writers on sentence-level technique, character, dialogue, plot, and the traditional publishing/query process; aimed at writers preparing manuscripts for agents and publishers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write what you must (compulsion principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: You have to find what you MUST write; when you find it you will know because the subject matter won't let you go.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't write simply to be published; be compelled by the idea. Riordan describes BIG RED TEQUILA as a book that 'took me by the throat' — this kind of compulsion is the signal you should follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain a reputable line edit / endorsement before querying
rubrics_metrics.description: A Bay Area creative writing teacher/author did a line edit and let Riordan use her name in the query letter; that 'foot in the door' helped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It can be helpful to pay someone reputable for a line edit. Look for freelance editors through local college writing institutes and get recommendations before paying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect and persist through rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejection is a part of writing; keep at it and don't give up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Riordan suggests 'wallpaper your room with rejection notes' if it helps; persistence and continued submission increase chances over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find a mentor and supportive critique group
rubrics_metrics.description: A young writer should find a mentor who believes in their talent; don't be afraid to ask for help.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find a teacher you respect, correspond with authors, or join a creative writing group — but choose one that's supportive and helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read a lot (immersion in other writers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Read everything you can to learn craft by immersion in voices, styles, and structures of writers who have gone before you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading widely helps you learn craft; don't worry about temporarily sounding like someone you admire — read more instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write every day (practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep a journal and write daily; writing is like a sport — you only get better if you practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jot down stories, descriptions, observations. If you stop practicing, the 'writing muscles' atrophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan ahead to avoid writer's block (road map/outline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Writer's block often happens because the writer hasn't planned where the book is going. Make a road map outlining where each chapter will go.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline doesn't have to be detailed and you can deviate, but planning ahead minimizes staring at a blank screen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finish the manuscript before abandoning it or over-revising
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't start another book when the middle gets hard; 'soldier through and finish.' Finish the manuscript, then revise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't worry about mistakes in the first draft. Finishing is necessary — very few can finish a book compared to writing a great first chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence-level competence (technical correctness and readability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most manuscripts are rejected because the writing is not technically competent: grammar must be correct and prose readable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Achieving sentence-level competence sets you apart from most submissions. Riordan provides sub-criteria and exercises to improve this level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence focus (appropriate subjects)
rubrics_metrics.description: The subjects of clauses should be appropriate to sentence content; favor concrete subjects over vague 'it' constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'It was a sunny day.' (vague) better as 'The sky was brilliant blue.' Exercise: underline subjects on a page and count abstractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modifiers (correct attachment and clear antecedents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modifiers should refer to the right thing — place modifiers close to the noun they modify; pronouns must have clear antecedents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of misplaced modifier: 'Can you help other writers who are writing books like me?' Better: 'Can you help other writers like me who are writing books?' Exercise: color-code phrases to match modifiers to what they modify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deft description (precise, purposeful detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose details carefully; description should be vivid but surgically precise and logically tied to plot or character. Avoid long lists of unrelated traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a uniting theme or extended metaphor for paragraph-length descriptions. Exercise: delete all adjectives and adverbs from a chapter, then add back sparingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallelism (consistent structure in lists/series)
rubrics_metrics.description: Items in a list should be similar in grammatical structure to avoid awkwardness and improve flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: change 'He likes dogs, hiking in the woods and reads books a lot' to 'He likes walking his dog, hiking in the woods, and reading lots of books.' Exercise: rewrite descriptions using parallel units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define characters primarily through action, then dialogue/description
rubrics_metrics.description: A character should be defined first through action, second through dialog and description, never through explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let choices and actions reveal character (responses to violence, love, etc.) rather than telling readers who the character is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be impressionist rather than realistic in character description
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a single deft stroke or striking metaphor to define a character rather than exhaustive lists of traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: instead of listing many traits, say 'She was a human tornado' and reinforce with a few supporting details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use real people as models but allow characters to develop independently
rubrics_metrics.description: It's natural to base characters on real people, but don't be constrained by the model — let characters evolve beyond the real-life inspiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't force the character to act exactly like the person they were modeled on; allow fictional autonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't tell the reader everything you know about a character
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit irrelevant details (e.g., eye color, college) unless they matter to the story; leave them in your subconscious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If stuck, fill out a character profile or journal in the character's voice to discover what matters to the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters must act (agency) — avoid passive characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters must make conscious choices and exert influence; a character who only receives events won't compel readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot should arise from characters' decisions. Coincidence is taboo — prefer cause and effect. Readers care because they see and judge characters' choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use character profiles to deepen understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a detailed character profile (name, age, background, quirks, fears, goals, etc.) to understand motives and uniqueness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Riordan provides a long worksheet of fields to fill out; use it to learn which facts matter to the story and which should remain subconscious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give each character a distinct voice
rubrics_metrics.description: No two characters should sound the same; readers should be able to identify speakers by voice alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate voices with dialect (lightly), favorite colloquialisms, speech patterns, and signature phrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid authorial intrusion in dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Let characters talk; minimize descriptive padding and tags.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tags only to delineate speakers ('John said.') or to slow pace/deliver unspoken info, or when a first-person narrator filters dialog. Keep tags simple and sparse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compress dialogue (economy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trim dialogue to the critical parts; realistic-sounding dialogue is often shortened and abridged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cut throw-away lines. Example: replace long hedged speech with the essential question or sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show only the dialogue that needs to be shown
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid mundane, repetitive, or already-known material in dialogue; zoom to the part the reader needs to hear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a character must catch another up, summarize instead ('I caught him up on what had happened.') and fast-forward to the interesting part.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dialogue to display conflict, not to impart information to the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue should reveal character and conflict; avoid making characters speak to the audience rather than to each other ('false triangle').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure speakers have opposing agendas so lines reveal character and tension rather than dump exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't write parts the reader would skip
rubrics_metrics.description: Elmore Leonard's maxim: omit what readers would skip — zoom in on what they want to see and leave out the rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-explaining. Keep scenes focused on what moves the story or reveals character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish mystery from confusion (manage information balance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep readers guessing but not confused: provide enough information to engage without giving away everything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build plot in layers of compelling questions. The reader should always have at least one question in mind that drives them forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get going — start with the dilemma (avoid limp openings/prologues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin with the central dilemma or action; chapter one should get to the point rather than excessive set-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes manuscripts are better if they start with chapter two. Avoid delaying action with prologues or overlong introductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the moral dilemma driving the novel
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful novel deals with an ethical or moral dilemma that haunts readers and makes them consider what they'd do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surface plot (kidnapping, romance) may hold attention briefly; only a moral dilemma sustains a whole novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure protagonist and antagonist exert influence (active conflict and causality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Protagonist must exert influence to solve the problem and antagonist must exert influence to stop the solution; the book must be about conscious choices and active conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid plots driven by random events. Emphasize cause-and-effect and agency on both sides of the conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have realistic expectations about publishing odds and income
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional-publishing odds are long: surveys cited (e.g., 3 manuscripts out of 10,000 published) and average published-writer incomes are low.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write because you have to, not because you expect to get rich. E-books/self-publishing rarely provide a shortcut — most sell fewer than 100 copies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase your odds by improving craft and professional behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: You can increase chances by writing well (technical competence), being businesslike, persistent, open to reasonable criticism, not submitting too soon, and targeting submissions well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use resources like WRITER'S MARKET or LITERARY AGENTS GUIDE to find appropriate agents; check agent preferences; be polite and professional in communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow a stepwise submission process (queries → samples → manuscript → agent selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: 1) Make sure manuscript is finished. 2) Send query letters/emails to agents (10–20 to start) according to their stated preferences. 3) If asked, send sample chapters and a one-page plot synopsis. 4) If asked, send full manuscript. 5) If represented, evaluate agent and then let agent submit to publishers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Query letter should introduce yourself, explain the book, offer sample chapters/plot synopsis, and include a SASE if sent by mail. Honor agent preferences for email vs. mail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only send additional materials when explicitly requested
rubrics_metrics.description: Send sample chapters or the full manuscript ONLY if and when an agent asks for them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces wasted effort and respects professional norms; typical request is first three chapters or first fifty pages and a short synopsis (no more than a page).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose an agent carefully and use professional resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether an agent is someone you can work with; agents earn commissions by getting fair hearings, advising on contracts, and selling foreign rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to the Association of Authors' Representatives for more information and use reference works to target agents who represent your kind of work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-publishing is possible but not an easy shortcut
rubrics_metrics.description: E-publishing can get you noticed in rare cases, but most e-books sell very few copies and self-publishing is not necessarily easier than traditional routes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand trade-offs and realistic chances of breakout success when considering self-publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be businesslike, polite, and targeted in submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Agents and editors appreciate a businesslike approach; target agents who represent your type of work and honor their submission preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft a concise one-page query, tailor submissions, and consult agent/publisher listings to ensure good matches.
